blocks.text: **The problem.** An alien language uses lowercase English letters in an unknown order. You're given a list of `words` that is **sorted** by that order, the way a dictionary is. Return a string of all the letters that appear, in an order consistent with the list. If several orders work, return any. If the list can't be sorted by any order, return `""`.

blocks.alt: Five sorted words: wrt, wrf, er, ett, rftt. Each neighbouring pair gives one clue from its first different letter: t before f, w before e, r before t, e before r. The clues form the chain w, e, r, t, f, which is the alphabet.

words = ["wrt","wrf","er","ett","rftt"]  ->  "wertf"
words = ["z","x"]                        ->  "zx"
words = ["z","x","z"]                    ->  ""     (z before x, and x before z)
words = ["abc","ab"]                     ->  ""     (a word can't come after its own prefix)

blocks.text: The idea: turn the word list into arrows

This is Course Schedule with letters — the hard part is finding the arrows. Compare each word with the **next** one. Walk along both until the first position where they differ: there, the letter in the first word comes **before** the letter in the second. That is the **only** clue the pair gives: letters after the first difference say nothing, because the words were already decided there.

Two traps. First, if a word is followed by its own **prefix** (`"abc"` then `"ab"`), no alphabet can sort them — the shorter word always comes first — so return `""`. Second, the clues can contradict each other in a **cycle** (`z` before `x` before `z`). The topological sort catches that: some letters never become ready.
Only neighbouring pairs need comparing. If `a` comes before `b` and `b` before `c`, the clue between `a` and `c` follows from the other two.
1. Build the graph, then Kahn's algorithm

Every letter that appears is a vertex, even one that never shows up in a clue — it still belongs in the answer. Add an arrow per clue (skip repeats, so in-degrees stay right), then take letters with no arrows coming in, exactly like ready courses.

blocks.caption: First the word pairs give the arrows, then letters are placed as they become ready. Try the contradiction and the prefix trap.

blocks.text: **Time O(C), space O(1).** C is the total number of characters in all the words: building the graph reads each character at most twice. The graph has at most 26 letters and 26 · 25 arrows, so the sort itself and all the memory are bounded by a constant.

The same arrows, sorted with the three-state DFS from Course Schedule II: a letter finishes after every letter that must come after it, so the finishing order reversed is the alphabet. An arrow back onto the current path is a contradiction.
**Time O(C), space O(1).** The same graph-building pass, and a DFS over at most 26 letters. The recursion is at most 26 calls deep.

blocks.text: Building the graph is where interviews are won or lost: one clue per neighbouring pair, from the first difference only, and the prefix check. After that, either sort works.

items: **A single word** — no clues at all, so any order of its letters is right.
**A word followed by its own prefix** — `["abc","ab"]` is impossible: return `""`.
**Letters that appear in no clue** — they must still be in the answer.
**The same clue twice** — add the arrow once, or the in-degree will be too high and the letter never becomes ready.
**Verifying an Alien Dictionary** — the alphabet is given; just check each neighbouring pair is in order.
**Sequence Reconstruction** — is there exactly **one** topological order? Only if the queue never holds more than one vertex at a time.
**Course Schedule II** — the same sort with the arrows handed to you. Previous lesson.
